theme: Don’t be taken captive; the new self; let Christ’s word dwell
readingInstruction: Read Colossians 2:6-3:17. Paul warns against being taken captive by empty philosophy and then gives the positive vision: you have died and been raised with Christ, so put off the old and put on the new. Read 3:1-17 slowly, as a portrait of the Christian life.
settingTheScene: After exalting Christ in chapter 1, Paul addresses the false teaching in Colosse. It seems to have included regulations about food, drink, festivals, and Sabbaths; visions and worship of angels; and severe treatment of the body. Paul’s answer is that all of this is only a shadow, and the substance is Christ. Then he turns to the new life, which is based on union with Christ in his death and resurrection.
observation: “See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition” (2:8).
“For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (2:9).
“By canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands” (2:14).
“These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (2:17).
“If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (3:1).
“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (3:3).
“And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony” (3:14).
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom” (3:16).
interpretation:
Paul begins with the basic instruction: “As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.” The Christian life continues as it began: with Christ. Then the warning: “See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.” Not all philosophy is wrong, but any teaching that adds to or displaces Christ is empty. The reason: “For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.” If you have Christ, you have everything.

Next, what Christ has done. In him you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God. “And you, who were dead in your trespasses… God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.” The debt-record that condemned us was nailed to the cross. “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.” The powers have been defeated.

So Paul says: “Let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” The old covenant regulations pointed forward to Christ, and now that the reality has come, we are not bound to the shadow. This is a significant text in understanding the relationship between the covenants. Christians differ on how it bears on the Sabbath, but all agree it clarifies that no ritual observance contributes to our standing before God. Rules that appear wise, like “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch,” have no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.

Chapter 3 begins with “If then you have been raised with Christ.” The resurrection has practical consequences. “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” Our true life is secured in heaven.

Then the practical: “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” Put away anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, and lying. These belong to the old self. “Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony. And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts.” Finally, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”
connection: Romans 6:1-14 speaks of union with Christ in death and resurrection. Ephesians 4:17-32 and Galatians 5:16-26 are parallels on putting off and putting on. Isaiah 61:10 speaks of being clothed in righteousness. Hebrews 8:5, 10:1 describe the law as a shadow. Mark 7:14-23 shows Jesus on clean and unclean. Matthew 6:19-21 says set your treasure in heaven. 1 Peter 2:9 speaks of God’s chosen ones. Philippians 3:20-21 speaks of heavenly citizenship. Psalm 119:11 speaks of treasuring the word.
application:
Read Colossians 3:12-17 aloud as a list of clothes. Put on one piece today.

Set your mind on things above for a few minutes at the start of the day.

Ask what “rules” you have made that are not from Christ. Where do you trust a shadow?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that in him the whole fullness of deity dwells, and that you have been filled in him.
Ask him to help you set your mind on things above.
Ask him to let his word dwell in you richly.
